data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Safety is the strictly stronger property and the one the log must require. Safety subsumes idempotency: a safe operation is one whose retry is observationally indistinguishable from a single execution \u2014 both in its own result and in its effect on concurrent operations. Idempotency is merely the self-referential special case f(f(x))=f(x), which says nothing about interaction with other operations during replay.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the log is strictly sequential (no interleaving), safety's isolation guarantee is vacuous and idempotency suffices.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'safe' is defined narrowly as 'does not harm others' without requiring idempotency, then safety is weaker, not stronger.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cited definitions treat safety and idempotency as independent properties with neither subsuming the other, this candidate's hierarchy collapses.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"At-least-once delivery in an append-only log creates a scenario where retried operations interleave with other operations during replay. A purely idempotent operation (e.g., 'set x=1') is safe against self-duplication, but if a concurrent operation reads x between the first and duplicate application, the intermediate state may violate invariants. Safety guarantees that the retry is invisible to all observers, not just to the operation itself. The causal mechanism: safe retry \u2192 no observable intermediate state difference \u2192 deterministic replay produces identical state regardless of delivery multiplicity. Mere idempotency \u2192 no self-effect difference but possible observable intermediate states \u2192 replay may diverge under interleaving.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
